https://www.mediafax.ro/english/miruta-m.text: Miruță: Marine drone loaded with explosives destroyed by two Romanian F-16s in the Black Sea According to Minister Miruță, the drone was destroyed by the onboard cannon of a Romanian F-16 fighter jet after two fighter jets were scrambled and given the order to fire. “A naval drone was destroyed by the Romanian Army using the onboard cannon of a Romanian F-16 fighter jet a few moments ago, in the area of the Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea,” Radu Miruță stated. The minister specified that authorities were informed earlier this morning by the Coast Guard of the marine drone’s presence a few hundred meters from the gas extraction operations, within Romania’s exclusive economic zone, approximately 80 miles east of Constanța. A command center was established at the Ministry of National Defense, and, according to Miruță, a request was made at the NATO level for the Romanian Armed Forces to assume command. “Following the analyses conducted and in coordination with the President of Romania, in order to protect the lives of the several hundred people working on the platform and to secure critical infrastructure, the decision was made to destroy the drone,” the minister stated. To respond quickly, two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled with orders to engage. The drone, which was loaded with explosives, was safely destroyed. Radu Miruță also noted that Romanian authorities received official confirmation, through a direct communication channel with the Ukrainian side, that the drone was not of Ukrainian origin. The Ministry of National Defense has not yet confirmed that the drone was loaded with explosives The Ministry of National Defense reported that two F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force intervened on Thursday in response to a small maritime drone located in Romania’s Exclusive Economic Zone, near the Neptun Alpha platform, approximately 80 nautical miles east of Constanța. “One of the aircraft engaged the target and fired its onboard cannon at it, striking the target,” the Ministry of National Defense reported. The presence of the drifting maritime drone was reported around 6:28 a.m. by a commercial vessel, according to the Ministry of National Defense. “A Coast Guard vessel, with an EOD team from the Romanian Naval Forces on board, is heading toward the area where the maritime drone is located to conduct an inspection,” the Ministry of National Defense stated, without providing any details about the drone’s explosive payload. In fact, Acting Defense Minister Radu Miruță also edited his Facebook post to remove the information stating that the drone was loaded with explosives. Nicușor Dan: A race against time Romanian President Nicușor Dan congratulated the Romanian Army and the pilots of the two Romanian F-16 fighter jets on the success of the mission to destroy the maritime drone near the Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea. The president also commended the Coast Guard for its promptness in reporting the drone’s presence in the area. “A race against time, in which the top priority was protecting the lives of the people working on the platform and keeping critical infrastructure out of any potential danger. I strongly condemn the escalation of these types of irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation. We remain vigilant alongside our NATO allies to defend ourselves and repel such provocations,” President Nicușor Dan wrote on X. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317.text: Image source, Swedish Coast Guard Image caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022 By Sarah Rainsford Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent Published 6 hours ago Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children. Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks. But German police were already closing in on him. After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany. Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime â attacking civilian infrastructure â allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine". Both he and his country have denied any involvement. Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea. There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 â not yet in action, but already full â and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas. Both have been inoperable ever since. Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers. They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda. Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat. As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow. Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure. But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise. They went on following the forensic crumbs. Eventually they led to Ukraine. The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services. In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich. That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy. He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada â all dated after the Nord Stream attacks. But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected. Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him. By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert. Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs. The saboteurs None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions. But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them. "Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that." Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe. That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it. Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution. "Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out. The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution. Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence. "At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained. Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned". Image source, Omar Marques/Getty Images Image caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far. Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August. He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation. Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him. Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning. He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver. But he is a civilian. Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him. In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war". As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more." Croatia is a different matter. Political ripples The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg. After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop. It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv. It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone. When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that". This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further. "I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully. He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did." First in the dock Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial. Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated. Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot. He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023. His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing. They are not saying, though. And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either. His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up. I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot. Photograph: Sabur Rashid/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Weather tracker Environment Deadly floods hit Iraq as thunderstorms sweep across region Violent storms lash northern Iraq and parts of Iran, while Portugal faces strong winds and Japan braces for further snowfall Oliver Wyndham-Lewis and Magdalena Shopova for the MetDesk Mon 9 Nov 2026 05.59 EST Last modified on Mon 9 Nov 2026 06.01 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Deadly flash floods hit northern Iraq on Saturday as severe thunderstorms swept across the region, including in neighbouring Iran. The city of Erbil, in Iraq, was particularly badly hit, with extensive damage to homes and businesses. Streets were inundated as torrential rain fell over a short period. Rainfall exceeded forecasts, with an estimated 80mm falling in the city, compared with expectations of 30mm. Two people were killed in the floods. In Europe, Storm Bruna is forecast to bring strong winds to Portugal this week, particularly along the west coast. Gusts are expected to reach 50mph (80km/h), with heavy rain and thunderstorms also expected. The total rainfall could reach 200mm by the end of the week. The storm has already affected the Canary Islands, where Tenerife recorded a gust of 80mph on Saturday night. Japan experienced a cold and snowy end to last week, with further snowfall expected in Hokkaido and parts of the mountains in the main island Honshu. Temperatures in Japan are forecast to fall below the seasonal average early this week, with Sapporo, the capital of Hokkaido prefecture, expected to plunge to 10C below average. Maximum temperatures in the city are likely to be about 4-6C on Monday and Wednesday, while Tuesday’s high is forecast to be about 0C. Minimum temperatures could fall to -6C by Wednesday, and -8C in other western parts of Hokkaido on Tuesday. Ski resorts are preparing for visitors after snowfall began on Friday. Total snowfall is expected to reach 30-50cm around Kiroro and Niesko, with about 20-30cm in Furano, Rusutsu and Sapporo. Other resorts could receive up to 20cm of snow by Wednesday. Strong winds accompanied the snow on Friday and over the weekend, with gusts of about 75mph in Kiroko and Niesko. During the strong El Niño, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific were about 3.5C above the climatological average at their peak in late October. As a result, Peru has been experiencing air temperatures 5-10C above the seasonal average. The unusually warm conditions expected to continue into next week. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.text: Image source, Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) Image caption, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has signalled his intention to run for president in the next elections By Wycliffe Muia Published 4 hours ago In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief. Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks. The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades. Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party. This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position. The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false". This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions. Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account. At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures. A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency. Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal. Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership. In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues". He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time". Image source, Ugandan presidency/X Image caption, President Yoweri Museveni's grandson (standing up, shaking the president's hand) has joined the army, alongside his father (sitting down, wearing camouflage) Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project". "Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC. He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question. Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness. The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu , has brought the crackdown into sharper focus. The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region. His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted. "The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X. He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested. The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post. The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations. Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper. They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations. This army chief threatened to castrate opposition leader and claimed descent from Jesus Published 31 January The 'shadow army' helping Uganda's long-serving president keep an iron grip on power Published 17 October 2025 The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter Published 30 October 2022 Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption. He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him. Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor. His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him. Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications. The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces. Image source, Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) Image caption, Maj Gen James Birungi was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge. He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive. "Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done." But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted. "The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says. He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession. The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released. Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings. "Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds. He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba. Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash". Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy. On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job. "Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted. He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy. The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible. It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it. Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly. Image source, Ugandan vice-presidency office/X Image caption, Vice-President Jessica Alupo is yet to respond to Gen Kainerugaba's posts questioning her loyalty Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability. Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics. He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party. Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations. Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army. Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power. "The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds. At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war. He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year , extending his rule into a fifth decade. Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end. He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership. But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated. At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported. Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership. There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president. Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation. Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion. He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition. "The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says. The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify. The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy. The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition. Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies. Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba . The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability. For now, Museveni remains in power. But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.
